d.chapter: Economic Geography — Natural Regions: 3. Desert Regions
d.notions: Xerophyte, succulent, ephemeral plant, desert soil, salinity, humus.
d.focus: Characteristics of the soils and vegetation of hot deserts.
d.competence: Learners are able to explain how plants survive with very little water, and to choose plants that resist drought for their homes.
objectives: Describe the vegetation of hot deserts.
Explain how desert plants are adapted to the lack of water.
Describe the soils of hot deserts.
recall: Hot deserts receive less than 250 mm of rain per year.
Days are very hot, nights are cold, and the air is very dry.
Hot, dusty winds and sandstorms are common.
d.recallNote: Check the homework: adaptations of a cactus, an acacia or a date palm.
situation: Fanta planted a mango tree and a small cactus in front of her house in Garoua at the start of the dry season. She forgot to water them for three months.
In March, the mango tree was dead, but the cactus was still green and healthy. Fanta wonders how the cactus survived without water.
sitQA: What is the problem raised in the situation above?
The problem is that Fanta does not understand how the cactus survived three months without water, while the mango tree died.
Which plant survived, and which plant died?
The cactus survived, but the mango tree died.
What can Fanta do to keep her plants alive in the dry season?
She can water them regularly, cover the soil with dry grass, or choose plants that resist drought.
d.justification: This lesson will help us to understand how desert plants survive with very little water, and what desert soils are like.

qa.q: In hot deserts, plants grow far apart and large areas have no plants at all. Why?
qa.a: There is very little water, so the few plants grow far apart to share the little water in the soil.

qa.q: The cactus has a thick, fleshy stem and spines instead of leaves. How do these help it to survive?
qa.a: The thick stem stores water, and the spines lose very little water. They also protect the plant from animals.

qa.q: Some desert plants have roots more than 20 metres long. Why?
qa.a: Long roots reach water deep under the ground. Other plants have wide roots near the surface to catch rain quickly.

qa.q: After a rare rain, the desert suddenly becomes green with flowers for a few weeks. How is this possible?
qa.a: Some plants, called ephemerals, have seeds that wait in the soil for years. After rain, they grow, flower and make new seeds very quickly.

sum.title: I. Vegetation
defs: A xerophyte is a plant that is adapted to live with very little water.
sum.intro: The vegetation of hot deserts is very scarce. Its main plants are cacti, thorny bushes such as acacias, tamarisks, grasses and date palms in oases.
items: A. Water Storage
Succulent plants, such as cacti, store water in their thick stems or leaves.
B. Reduced Water Loss
Plants have small, waxy leaves or spines instead of leaves, so they lose very little water.
C. Long or Wide Roots
Some plants have very long roots to reach deep water. Others have wide roots near the surface.
D. Short Life Cycle
Ephemeral plants grow, flower and make seeds in a few weeks after a rare rain.

qa.q: There are very few plants in the desert. What does this mean for the amount of humus in the soil?
qa.a: Desert soils have very little humus, because few plants die and rot in them.

qa.q: The strong sun makes water evaporate from the soil and leaves salt on the surface. What problem does this cause?
qa.a: The soil becomes salty, and most crops cannot grow in salty soil. This is called salinisation.

qa.q: Along the Nile, in the middle of the desert, farmers grow rich crops. What does this show about desert soils?
qa.a: It shows that some desert soils can be fertile when they receive water. The Nile also brings fertile mud, called alluvium.

sum.title: II. Soils
sum.intro: The soils of hot deserts have the following characteristics:
items: A. Sandy or Stony
Desert soils are thin, sandy or stony, and they hold little water.
B. Little Humus
They contain little humus, because there are few plants.
C. Salty Soils
Evaporation leaves salt on the surface, so some soils are salty.
D. Fertile with Water
Some desert soils become fertile when they are irrigated, as along the Nile.

evaluation: What is a xerophyte? Give one example.
A xerophyte is a plant adapted to live with very little water, like the cactus.
Give two ways in which desert plants reduce water loss.
They have small, waxy leaves or spines instead of leaves.
Why are desert soils often salty?
They are salty because evaporation leaves salt on the surface of the soil.
remediation: A plant adapted to very little water is a ______.
The cactus stores water in its ______.
Plants that grow and flower quickly after rain are called ______.
Desert soils contain little ______, because there are few plants.
When evaporation leaves salt in the soil, it is called ______.
Desert soils can be fertile when they are ______.
d.remediationAnswers: 1. xerophyte 2. stem 3. ephemerals 4. humus 5. salinisation 6. irrigated
